text: ArgoCD bundles where config comes from, where it goes, and how to reconcile it into one Application object. Flux takes a different approach: it splits the same job into small, composable resources that each do one thing and reference each other by name. Learning to read those pieces separately is the key to reading any Flux setup.

A GitRepository is Flux's Source resource. It tells the source-controller to clone a repo, poll it on an interval — here, every minute — and expose the result as an artifact that other resources can point at. Notice what it doesn't do: it never applies anything to the cluster by itself. That separation means one GitRepository can feed several different reconcilers without re-cloning for each one.

A Flux Kustomization resource is the piece that actually does something with a source. Its sourceRef points back at the GitRepository by name, and its path names the directory to run a Kustomize build against — typically an environment overlay, the same pattern you'll use in the next lesson. Prune true deletes resources that were removed from that path in Git, so cleanup happens automatically instead of leaving orphans running.

HelmRelease extends the exact same pattern to Helm charts. Instead of a GitRepository, it references a HelmRepository — the chart index — and Flux's helm-controller fetches the named chart and version, renders it with the values block, and installs or upgrades it. That's the declarative, Git-driven version of running helm install or helm upgrade from a laptop: the chart version and every value are committed and reviewed, not typed once and forgotten.

Source, Kustomization, and HelmRelease each reconcile independently and show up as their own status with commands like flux get kustomizations — more pieces to read, but each one composable on its own. Next lesson turns to a question both ArgoCD and Flux assume you've already answered: how do you actually lay out the Git repository itself across dev, staging, and prod?
